lead: The Bayes optimal classifier is the best possible classifier when you know the posterior over hypotheses. It does not pick one hypothesis. It lets every hypothesis vote for a label, and weights each vote by P(h|D), the probability that h is correct after seeing training data D. The result is P(c|x,D), the posterior probability of label c for test input x. It is an ideal because the full hypothesis space is usually too large to sum over. Gibbs is a randomised shortcut: draw one hypothesis from P(h|D) and predict with it. Bayesian learning theory uses both to reason about optimal and sampled decisions.
prereq: You need: Bayes theorem and posterior probability from 3.2.

blocks.text: Let H be the set of all hypotheses under consideration. A hypothesis h is one possible classifier, such as one decision tree or one set of parameter values. After training on data D, Bayesian learning gives a posterior P(h|D) for each h. The Bayes optimal classifier does not choose one h. It asks: for a test input x, what is the probability of each label c?

blocks.where: h is a hypothesis; H is the hypothesis space; D is the training data; x is the test input; c is a class label; P(h|D) is the posterior weight of h; P(c|x,h) is the vote of h for label c. For a deterministic classifier it is 1 when h predicts c and 0 otherwise.

blocks.text: The sum adds the posterior weights of all hypotheses that vote for c. The prediction is the label with the largest P(c|x,D). For two labels, P(No|x,D) = 1 - P(Yes|x,D). This is averaging over the whole hypothesis space, so it is an ideal. It is not the MAP hypothesis, which is argmax_h P(h|D). MAP keeps the single most probable h; Bayes optimal lets all h vote.
Gibbs algorithm is a randomised approximation. It draws one hypothesis h at random from the posterior P(h|D), then predicts h(x) for the test input x. The sampling rule is the whole algorithm.

items: Compute or obtain the posterior P(h|D) for every hypothesis h in H.
Draw one hypothesis h at random, with probability P(h|D).
Use that one hypothesis to predict the label h(x) for the test input x.
Repeat the draw for another prediction if a fresh random choice is wanted.

blocks.text: In the three-hypothesis example, h1 is drawn with probability 0.5, h2 with 0.3, h3 with 0.2. A different run may draw a different hypothesis. If h1 is drawn, the prediction is Yes; h2 gives No; h3 gives Yes. So Gibbs predicts Yes with probability 0.7 and No with 0.3. It is not a majority vote over hypotheses. It is also not sampling the label from P(c|x,D); it samples a hypothesis and then uses that hypothesis. Only a few universities teach Gibbs in detail, so know the sampling rule and that it is randomized.

Why use an ideal that cannot be computed? It gives a target. The Bayes optimal error is the smallest possible average 0-1 error for the given hypothesis space and prior. Any real classifier, such as Naive Bayes or a decision tree, can be compared with it in theory. The formula also explains model averaging: many models weighted by how likely they are after data can beat one model. Ensembles do this in practice, but they are not exact Bayes optimal; see 3.8. In real problems the sum over H is too large, so we approximate by sampling, variational methods or a single MAP model. The Bayes optimal classifier also reminds us that uncertainty over hypotheses matters. A confident MAP model can be wrong when many less likely hypotheses vote for another label.

examples.question: Three hypotheses remain after training: P(h1|D)=0.5, P(h2|D)=0.3, P(h3|D)=0.2. On a test input x, h1 and h3 predict Yes, while h2 predicts No. (a) Compute the Bayes optimal posterior P(Yes|x,D) and P(No|x,D), and state the predicted label. (b) For the Gibbs algorithm, give the probability that it predicts Yes and No. (c) Explain why the Gibbs answer is not a new posterior calculation.
steps: Bayes optimal sums posterior weights of hypotheses that vote Yes. The Yes-voters are h1 and h3.
The larger value is 0.7, so Bayes optimal predicts Yes.
Gibbs draws one hypothesis with probabilities P(h1|D)=0.5, P(h2|D)=0.3, P(h3|D)=0.2. It predicts Yes when h1 or h3 is drawn: 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7. It predicts No when h2 is drawn: 0.3.
Gibbs does not compute a posterior over labels. It samples a hypothesis and uses that hypothesis; the Yes probability 0.7 is the total posterior mass of hypotheses that output Yes.
examples.answer: Bayes optimal predicts Yes with P(Yes|x,D)=0.7 and P(No|x,D)=0.3; Gibbs predicts Yes with probability 0.7 and No with probability 0.3.

traps: Bayes optimal is not the MAP hypothesis. MAP picks the single most probable h; Bayes optimal averages every h and may choose a different label.
Gibbs is not majority vote. It draws one hypothesis from the posterior and uses that hypothesis; its prediction is random across runs.
P(c|x,D) is a posterior probability over labels, not over hypotheses. Do not sum P(h|D) as if it were P(c|D).
A high posterior for one hypothesis does not make it the Bayes optimal label for every x. The vote P(c|x,h) depends on x.
Do not confuse Bayes optimal classifier with Naive Bayes. Naive Bayes is one restricted hypothesis with an independence assumption.

quiz.q: Write the Bayes optimal formula for P(c|x,D) and define each symbol.
quiz.a: P(c|x,D) = Σ_h P(c|x,h) P(h|D). h is a hypothesis, H is the hypothesis space, D is training data, x is the test input, c is a label, P(h|D) is the posterior weight, and P(c|x,h) is the vote of h for c.

quiz.q: Why is the Bayes optimal classifier usually not trained as a normal model?
quiz.a: It must sum over every hypothesis in H, weighted by P(h|D). The hypothesis space is usually huge, and the exact posterior is hard to compute. It is an ideal benchmark, not a usual trained classifier.

quiz.q: Posteriors are P(h1|D)=0.6 and P(h2|D)=0.4. h1 predicts A; h2 predicts B. Find Bayes optimal P(A|x,D), P(B|x,D) and the prediction.
quiz.a: P(A|x,D)=0.6, P(B|x,D)=0.4. The larger is 0.6, so Bayes optimal predicts A.

quiz.q: Posteriors are P(h1|D)=0.4, P(h2|D)=0.35, P(h3|D)=0.25. h1 and h2 predict Yes; h3 predicts No. Find the Bayes optimal prediction and the probability that Gibbs predicts Yes.
quiz.a: P(Yes|x,D)=0.4+0.35=0.75. P(No|x,D)=0.25. Bayes optimal predicts Yes. Gibbs predicts Yes with probability 0.75, since it draws h1 or h2 with total probability 0.75.

quiz.q: Compare the Bayes optimal classifier and Gibbs algorithm in one paragraph.
quiz.a: Bayes optimal weights every hypothesis by its posterior and predicts the label with the largest total weight. Gibbs samples one hypothesis from the posterior and predicts with that hypothesis. Bayes optimal is deterministic for fixed posteriors and votes; Gibbs is randomized and can differ from run to run. Gibbs is not a majority vote.

quiz.q: What exactly does Gibbs sample? Does it sample a label directly from P(c|x,D)?
quiz.a: Gibbs samples one hypothesis h from P(h|D). It then uses h to predict. It does not directly sample the label from P(c|x,D).

quiz.q: State one difference between MAP and Bayes optimal.
quiz.a: MAP chooses the single hypothesis h with the largest P(h|D). Bayes optimal sums the votes of all hypotheses weighted by P(h|D), then chooses the label with the largest total.

beyond: Not for the exam. Bayesian model averaging is common in probabilistic machine learning, where many models are weighted by posterior probability instead of keeping one. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods sample from posterior distributions when exact sums are impossible; Gibbs sampling is a related sampler, though the Gibbs algorithm here is a classifier rule, not the sampler. Search terms: Bayesian model averaging, posterior predictive distribution, Gibbs sampling, PAC-Bayes bounds.
